summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The national framework is what binds the Ica region: no trans-specific regional statute, ordinance or administrative rule has been recorded for Ica, so entry, documents, facilities and policing are governed by national law and national practice.

In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and the text bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. On 2 April 2025 the Plenary approved the bill and exempted it from a second vote; its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for those narrow exceptions, and the wider legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, holds in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination guarantee of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches both public and private life. A visitor can be refused entry to a restroom matching their gender identity, and LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that access will turn on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks; she notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of whom 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with multiple gunshots or stabbings. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.
tangentialFactors:
Recorded figures understate the scale. A 2024 report co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded hate-crime figures are only a sub-registry, so the documented killings and violations represent reported cases rather than a count of incidents.

The comparative position is unusually weak. After the 2017 repeal, Peru stands with Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, while the Inter-American framework moves in the opposite direction through Advisory Opinion OC-24/17.

Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people, an assessment that frames how the April 2025 provisions are likely to be applied in practice.

IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, evidence of the official register in which the facility restrictions were debated.

The bathroom dispute originates in a complaint about an airport in Lima rather than in Ica, but the resulting statute is national and applies to every region's facilities, transport hubs and public buildings.
localsOnly:
Health-care settings moved in a protective direction. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The 2017 repeal followed an April Constitutional Committee vote and was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members amid a petition claiming one million signatures.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years.

The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI's 170 recorded rights-violation cases over 2020-2023 include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias lodged in 2020 alone. The 170 cases and 54 homicides cover Peru as a whole rather than Ica.

Residents and long-term visitors must also contend with restroom enforcement by private operators, since a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym applying the policy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ica-specific record of enforcement of the April 2025 restroom provisions was available in the source inventory; whether police, municipal inspectors or private operators in Ica have applied article 5, and how frequently, remains unresolved.

The inventory provides no breakdown of the 54 homicides or 170 rights-violation cases by region, so the number recorded in Ica between 2020 and 2023 is not sourced here.

The gym complaint and the television harassment incident are documented at national level; whether comparable complaints or incidents have occurred in Ica is not sourced.

The sources do not indicate whether any court in Ica has reviewed the restroom provisions or the anti-equality decree, or how the July 2025 Lima ruling is being applied outside the capital.

Document and marker rules for trans visitors entering Peru, and the practice of Peruvian border and airport authorities on identity documents, are not covered by this inventory.
